author: Mo Qureshi
headline: Packaging capability constrains Saudi food export growth
deck: Export markets impose format, labelling and shelf-life requirements that a domestic packaging line was never specified to meet.
excerpt: Packaging capability rather than processing capacity is frequently the constraint on Saudi food manufacturers seeking export markets.
content:
Packaging machinery forms one of the declared sector divisions at Saudi Food Manufacturing in Jeddah at the end of September, alongside ingredients, processing, supply chain solutions and control and automation. For manufacturers with export ambitions it is the division that matters most, and the reason is not obvious from inside a domestic operation.

A food manufacturer selling into its home market optimises packaging for that market: the pack sizes retailers stock, the labelling its regulator requires, the shelf life its distribution chain demands. Every one of those changes at the border. Export markets want different formats, mandate different label content in different languages, and — because the distribution chain is longer — require materially longer shelf life than the same product needs at home.

Extending shelf life is a packaging engineering problem before it is a formulation one. Modified atmosphere packaging, higher-barrier films, aseptic filling and retort processing all extend product life, and each requires specific machinery. A line built to fill and seal for a domestic chilled chain cannot simply be reconfigured to produce an aseptic pack for a market three weeks away; it is a different machine.

That is why packaging capability, rather than processing capacity, is frequently the binding constraint on a food exporter. A plant may have ample capacity to make more product and no ability to package it in a form the target market accepts.

The German pavilion at the show is well populated on exactly this equipment. ROVEMA exhibits packaging machinery, Jokey packaging containers, HASSIA-REDATRON beverage machinery, and the processing builders SOLLICH, Chocotech, Röders and TRIMA cover confectionery and food processing. Multivac, among the named exhibitors, is a significant supplier of vacuum and modified atmosphere packaging systems.

Saudi Arabia's export ambition in food is real and documented — this publication has reported the wider industrial policy turn toward exports as the Kingdom's factory count passed 13,600, alongside the persistent weakness in export orders that has accompanied non-oil growth.

The freight economics sit behind it. Food is low value per tonne relative to its bulk, which makes shipping cost a large share of delivered price and puts nearby markets — the GCC, the Levant, East Africa — ahead of distant ones regardless of demand. Jeddah Islamic Port's position matters here, and this publication has reported Masdar Building Materials' logistics centre there and Mawani's wider logistics-centre programme.

Sector divisions and exhibitor names are taken from the organisers' published material. A manufacturer weighing export entry should cost the packaging line before it costs the marketing. Freight cost also compounds the format problem, because a pack optimised for a domestic chilled run is rarely the pack that travels economically.
